blocks.text: A cast steel wheel hub looks perfect on the outside, yet cutting it open reveals a ragged cavity deep inside the thick boss where the last liquid froze with nothing left to feed it. The cavity is not a mistake in the pour; it is a predictable result of the order in which different parts of the casting freeze, and you can predict that order with one equation.

blocks.markdown: When molten metal cools in a mould it solidifies from the mould wall inward. The time a casting needs to freeze depends on how much heat it must lose (proportional to its volume $V$) and how quickly it can lose it (proportional to the surface area $A$ in contact with the mould). Thick compact sections therefore freeze later than thin or sprawling ones, because their volume-to-area ratio is larger. Metal shrinks as it solidifies (typically several percent by volume for many alloys), so the last region to freeze needs a reservoir of liquid to feed it.

blocks.title: Chvorinov's rule
blocks.text: Chvorinov's rule states that total solidification time is $t_s=B\,(V/A)^2$, where $V$ is the casting volume, $A$ is the surface area through which heat escapes, and $B$ is the mould constant (s/mm$^2$ here). $B$ depends on the metal, the mould material and the pouring temperature, and is found from experience or a trial casting. The ratio $V/A$ has units of length and is sometimes called the casting modulus.

blocks.caption: Chvorinov's rule and the ratio form (same metal and mould)

blocks.title: Freezing time of a plate casting
blocks.prompt: A rectangular plate casting $200\times100\times20$ mm is made in a sand mould with $B=1.2$ s/mm$^2$ (a representative figure for a sand mould, not a handbook value). Assume all faces lose heat. Find $V/A$ and the freezing time.
blocks.answer: V/A is 7.69 mm and the plate takes about 71 s to solidify.

blocks.markdown: A **riser** (feeder) is a reservoir of liquid metal attached to the casting that supplies liquid to compensate shrinkage. For it to work, the riser must still be liquid when the casting has frozen, so the riser must solidify later. Using Chvorinov's rule with the same $B$, this means $(V/A)_{riser}>(V/A)_{casting}$. A common design practice is to require $(V/A)_{riser}\ge1.25\,(V/A)_{casting}$, which makes the riser freeze at least $1.25^2\approx1.56$ times longer. The riser should also hold enough metal to supply the shrinkage volume, which is checked separately.

blocks.title: Sizing a cylindrical riser
blocks.prompt: The plate above needs a cylindrical riser with height $H=1.5D$. Heat is lost from the riser's side and top only, since its base joins the casting. Using the 1.25 factor, find the minimum diameter and check the freezing times.

steps.text: Cylinder with $H=1.5D$: $V=0.375\pi D^3$, $A=\pi DH+\pi D^2/4=1.75\pi D^2$.
Check: riser freezing time versus casting.

blocks.answer: The riser must be at least about 45 mm in diameter and 67 mm tall; it freezes in about 111 s, 1.56 times as long as the casting.

blocks.caption: The main elements of a gating system

blocks.markdown: The **gating system** is the set of channels that carries metal from the ladle to the cavity. Metal falling a height $h$ accelerates to about $v=\sqrt{2gh}$ by Bernoulli's equation, and velocities of this size cause **turbulence**: the metal surface folds over itself, entraining oxide films and air bubbles as defects, and the flow can erode mould sand into the casting. Good gating keeps the velocity low, usually below about 0.5 m/s in the cavity entry for light alloys (a commonly quoted guideline), keeps channels full and fills from the bottom up.

blocks.title: Directional solidification
blocks.text: The goal is to have solidification progress from the thin, far-away regions toward the riser, so liquid feed is always available. Chvorinov's rule guides riser size, and chills (metal blocks in the mould) can be used to speed up freezing where a thick section is far from the riser.

blocks.title: Riser rule of thumb
blocks.text: The 1.25 factor is a typical safety allowance, not a physical law. The riser must also have enough volume to feed the casting's shrinkage, so check both the modulus and the volume. If a riser is too small, a shrinkage cavity forms inside the casting near the riser.

points: Chvorinov's rule $t_s=B(V/A)^2$ predicts that compact thick sections freeze later than thin ones.
A riser must freeze after the casting, so $(V/A)_{riser}\ge1.25(V/A)_{casting}$ is a common design target, plus enough volume to supply shrinkage.
Fluid velocity from a free fall of height $h$ is $v=\sqrt{2gh}$; tapered sprues, wells, chokes, filters and bottom gating limit turbulence.
Reducing turbulence prevents oxide entrainment, gas pick-up and sand erosion, giving cleaner castings.

questions.stem: A casting is scaled up uniformly so that every linear dimension doubles. If metal and mould are unchanged, how does the Chvorinov solidification time change?

options.text: It doubles
It increases by a factor of 4
It increases by a factor of 8
It is unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: It increases by a factor of 4

distractorRationale.a: Time depends on the square of $V/A$, and $V/A$ itself doubles, so the factor is 4, not 2.
distractorRationale.c: Volume scales by 8 but time depends on $(V/A)^2$ not on $V$, so 8 overstates it.
distractorRationale.d: A larger casting holds more heat per unit surface, so it freezes more slowly.

questions.explanation: Doubling every dimension multiplies volume by 8 and area by 4, so $V/A$ doubles. Since $t_s=B(V/A)^2$, the freezing time is multiplied by $2^2=4$.

questions.stem: A steel cube casting of side 80 mm is made in a mould with $B=1.5$ s/mm$^2$. Assuming all six faces lose heat, calculate the solidification time in seconds.
A casting with $V/A=8$ mm freezes in 90 s in a given sand mould. A second casting of the same metal in the same mould has $V/A=12$ mm. What freezing time do you expect?

options.text: About 135 s
About 60 s
About 40 s
About 202 s

distractorRationale.a: This scales the time linearly with $V/A$ (90 times 1.5), but the rule uses the square.
distractorRationale.b: This takes the inverse ratio, as if a larger section froze faster.
distractorRationale.c: This inverts and squares the ratio (90 times 0.444), again the wrong direction.

questions.explanation: By the ratio form, $t_2=90(12/8)^2=90(2.25)=202.5$ s. The larger modulus gives a much longer time because of the square.

questions.stem: A cubic casting of side 100 mm needs a cylindrical riser with height equal to diameter, losing heat from its side and top (so $V/A=D/5$). The riser must have a modulus at least 1.25 times that of the casting (all six faces of the cube lose heat). Calculate the minimum riser diameter in mm.
questions.explanation: The cube modulus is $100/6=16.67$ mm, so the riser needs $(V/A)_r\ge1.25\times16.67=20.83$ mm. For $H=D$, $V=\pi D^3/4$ and $A=\pi D^2+\pi D^2/4=1.25\pi D^2$, so $V/A=D/5$. Hence $D\ge5\times20.83=104.2$ mm.

questions.stem: Why must a riser be designed to solidify later than the casting it feeds?

options.text: So liquid metal is still available to replace shrinkage until the casting is solid
So it can be cut off more easily
So it can act as a chill
So that it makes the casting stronger by remelting

questions.correctOptionText: So liquid metal is still available to replace shrinkage until the casting is solid

distractorRationale.b: Removal is a secondary issue and does not drive the freezing order.
distractorRationale.c: A chill speeds up freezing; the riser should do the opposite.
distractorRationale.d: Remelting is not the purpose; the riser supplies liquid, it does not remelt solid metal.

questions.explanation: As the casting solidifies it contracts, and the contraction must be supplied with liquid metal through a still-open feed path. If the riser freezes first, the shrinkage appears as a cavity in the casting instead.

questions.stem: For a given riser volume, which shape will freeze latest, meeting the aim of a large modulus?

options.text: A long thin cylinder with $H/D=6$
A thin flat plate
A compact shape such as a sphere or a squat cylinder with $H/D$ about 1 to 1.5
A shape with many fins to cool it

questions.correctOptionText: A compact shape such as a sphere or a squat cylinder with $H/D$ about 1 to 1.5

distractorRationale.a: A tall thin cylinder has a large surface area for its volume and so a small modulus.
distractorRationale.b: A plate has a very high area-to-volume ratio and freezes quickly.
distractorRationale.d: Fins increase area and speed up freezing.

questions.explanation: Freezing time grows with $V/A$, so the best riser has the smallest surface area for its volume. A sphere is ideal and squat cylinders with $H/D$ around 1 to 1.5 are close to it and easier to mould.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a tapered sprue in a gating system?

options.text: To increase the metal velocity as much as possible
To act as a riser
To chill the metal
To keep the sprue full so air is not drawn into the metal stream

questions.correctOptionText: To keep the sprue full so air is not drawn into the metal stream

distractorRationale.a: Higher velocity worsens turbulence and oxide entrainment; the taper compensates for acceleration.
distractorRationale.b: Risers feed shrinkage and are separate parts of the mould.
distractorRationale.c: Chilling is not a function of the sprue.

questions.explanation: Metal accelerates as it falls, so the stream would contract and detach from a straight-walled sprue, drawing air in. A taper matching the contracting stream keeps it full and prevents aspiration.

questions.stem: Metal is poured down a sprue so that the free fall height from the pouring basin to the sprue base is 0.40 m. Using Bernoulli's equation with no losses, calculate the metal velocity at the base in m/s.
questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives $v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(9.81)(0.40)}=2.80$ m/s. This ideal velocity is far above the roughly 0.5 m/s desired at the cavity entry, which is why the system uses a choke, wells and bottom gates to slow the metal.

questions.stem: Describe four features of a well-designed gating system and explain how each reduces turbulence or the entry of inclusions into the casting.
markingGuide: Tapered sprue keeps full flow, prevents air aspiration
Sprue well or runner extension traps the first dirty metal and absorbs energy
Choke area sets filling rate and keeps channels full
Filters or bottom/side gating trap oxide and fill quietly, avoiding free-fall splashing
Links reduced turbulence to fewer oxide films, gas entrainment and less mould erosion
questions.explanation: A gating system reduces velocity and keeps channels full so the metal does not splash or entrain air. Wells and filters trap oxide and slag before they reach the cavity.

questions.stem: A casting has a thick boss connected to a thin flange. Explain, with Chvorinov's rule, where a shrinkage cavity is most likely to form and how a riser and a chill could be used to prevent it.
markingGuide: Thick boss has larger $V/A$ so freezes later than the flange
Isolated last-freezing region cannot be fed, so a shrinkage cavity forms there
Riser placed on the boss with $(V/A)_{riser}\ge1.25(V/A)_{boss}$ so liquid stays available
Chill near the boss (or far from the riser) speeds local freezing to encourage directional solidification
Check riser volume as well as modulus
questions.explanation: The boss freezes last and cannot draw liquid from the already solid flange, so a cavity forms there. A correctly sized riser on the boss and chills elsewhere create directional solidification toward the riser.
